Those two examples were young linebackers in their first year in a system, which is why this is a question for Jay, not a critique. Are the spies empowered to do more than we're seeing? Are there further iterations of spy where they act more like on-demand blitzers or robbers depending on what they see in the backfield? Usually I can guess at such things but I admit here's where my lack of actual football experience fails me; spies are such a lost art in football that I've never seen them discussed in clinics or met a coach that uses them extensively beyond very low levels of football, so I don't know the thinking at this level.
What about last week when you declared MSU found the weakness?
I thought about writing a Sharpies—it's in the MGoBlog drafts and you got no content yesterday—to follow up on this. It had a nice introduction with Sam Sword in it. The impetus was Hill doing the thing I suggested works against Insert Iso: 3-4.

[link]

Michigan was 44% in odd fronts on standard downs in this game, a season high, and up from 23% against MSU. The only other game that saw so many odd fronts on standard downs was Oklahoma, whose OL was getting thrashed so thoroughly Michigan just went with a three DL for most of the game.
I assume this was a response to getting Iso'd against MSU. Odd fronts disrupt Iso by confusing which side of center is going to have more defenders, and which LB is actually the MIKE you need to slam a blocker into. A 3-4 defense can often afford to have their big nose guard two-gap the center, and if he ends up on one side the MIKE can take the other. You see that happen above. Oregon is running that Insert Trap variant where the TE hits Pierce when he comes upfield so the LG and C can combo down to Bowles.

Kanka playing right over the center makes this a tough read however. Does the LG stay on Kanka or work down to Bowles. They guess work down.

And then Kanka and Bowles use that knowledge to pop into the opposite gaps.

By staying in the middle of the center, Kanka really could have chosen either. If the LG stayed on him, that would just free Bowles to go wherever the RB did. If Oregon ever pulled out regular Iso I was planning to pull that and show the 3-4 against the base, but Oregon put their Insert game to bed afterwards in favor of Stretch and Power with two OL pulling.
Oregon wasn't really the team to Iso anyways. Their "fullback" is just another running back, and their idea of running the ball is mostly delivering a really good running back to someplace he can make people miss. Their big reveal for this game—running wise at least—was this Power Draw they ran the first time using a slot receiver as the RB and the actual RB as a tight end.
#6 on the top of the formation vs #90 Daley

[link]
Having a running back—an OREGON running back—try to block John Henry Daley was...a choice.
Speaking of choices, is Michigan a box or spill defense now?
They're both. I always thought you want to be one or the other, because if you ever confuse them you're giving up an explosive, but apparently this is normal for college teams right now. Also apparently it's fine if you have a great safety.
#7 safety on top

[link]

This approach is a major departure from the structure of the Ravens defense I'm most familiar with, so I don't yet have enough background to grade the subtle things that I picked up on from years of Mac/Minter/Martindale. But I can see why they made the change, at least on this side of the ball, because Bracy is the best player on the team and this gets him more involved. It sucks that such a great safety season is being wasted on such a throwaway year. He is the measuring stick for all future strong safeties the way Rod Moore in his prime will be the measuring stick for all free safeties.

Refs? Were fine. Some uncalled holding both ways. It took this long into the season to get a Refs+2 event, but if you asked me preseason where I'd like that to happen (other than Columbus) I would say 4th down in the endzone at Oregon in a one-score game is a good spot.
Heroes? Bracy. Daley. Lea'ea. Those who stay.
Maybe not so heroic? Chase Taylor will want to bury this film. Smith Snowden and Troy Bowles too.

What does it mean for UCLA and beyond?
Season's over. Grateful to anyone still playing, gonna take it all about as seriously as a bowl game from here.

michigan.headline: ‘Prideful’ Michigan Football seniors to play at The Big House one last time
michigan.body:
Rod Moore Jr. of the Michigan Wolverines enters the field before an NCAA football game at SHI Stadium in Piscataway, United States, on October 31, 2026. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

As Michigan Football limps into its home finale on Saturday against UCLA, Senior Day should provide some positive memories for this 2027 class.

Namely, the 2023 National Championship. Safety Rod Moore was the primary contributor out of those still in Ann Arbor, and cornerbacks Jyaire Hill and Zeke Berry and defensive lineman Enow Etta chipped in, too.

Head coach Kyle Whittingham expressed his gratitude for the seniors and their ability to keep the locker room “together” during this frustrating 2026 campaign.

“I would say that they’re very prideful. They’ve won a lot of games here. Most of them were here for the Championship Game. In fact, unless they transferred in the last couple of years, all of them were here. And so they had a chance to experience that, which is awesome,” Whittingham told the Inside Michigan Football radio show host Jon Jansen on Monday night.

“I mean how many guys get the chance to be national champs in college football? And so, they’ve had some really good experiences here. This year, of course, has been very different from what we all hoped it would be. But they’ve persevered. They have not splintered.”

For as easy as it would be to give up on this season, try telling a guy like Moore that these final two (potentially three) games are meaningless.

Yet as the year winds down and departures become a point of conversation, Whittingham had praise for Berry. Beyond his skills in the secondary, he has been a valuable asset on special teams.

“Zeke Berry, I think, is one of the best gunners in the country. And, you talk about making an NFL roster, it oftentimes comes down to guys that can play special teams, and Zeke is really helping his cause right now,” he said.

Cornerbacks coach Jernaro Gilford also had strong reviews on Berry, and his unit has been one of the brightest spots on the team. They did have their worst outing to date against the Ducks.

But handling defeat is part of the cornerback lifestyle.

“‘Everybody trains, everybody works just like you do,’” Gilford tells his group, “and at the end of the day, I’ll be naive to say that nobody’s going to catch a ball or nobody’s going to make a big play. I just kind of harp on telling our guys to make more plays than they give up.”

Gilford also has depth at his disposal. There are only so many snaps to go around with the aforementioned outside duo and nickelback Smith Snowden. However, there are still some enticing prospects in the pipeline.

One of whom is sophomore Shamari Earls.

“He’s developed. He’s gotten better and better. The thing that I want to see from him is consistency, man. And we preach it every single day, just being consistent in everything you do on and off the field, ‘cause it’s a combination of everything,” Gilford said.

Gilford said to keep an eye out for freshman Jamarion Vincent, too, who could emerge as a leader on the back end sooner than later.

“The main guy is going to be Jam,” Gilford said. “… Great frame, 6’2, can run, sticky in coverage. He’s very consistent as far as off the field. On the field, it just so happened he’s behind a guy like Suge (Jyaire Hill), and behind a guy like Zeke.”

Finally, sophomore punter Cam Brown joined the show to break down different punting techniques — such as the banana — and that punters do indeed watch film like everyone else.

“We do a lot of scouting and special teams, like, we know, like, how many balls someone’s dropped or, like, what type of kicks they’ve dropped. So, that really comes into play,” Brown said.

Brown will not be among those honored during the pregame ceremony, but it does provide the seniors one last chance to show out at the Big House.

Do you think the Wolverines can play spoiler and ruin the Bruins’ undefeated season? Or was the Oregon defeat simply another nail in the coffin? Let us know your thoughts down below.

msu.headline: Spartans Look to Bounce Back, Again
msu.body:
EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks rushes the ball during the 1st half of a game between the Michigan Wolverines and Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

I mean, I guess nobody has to worry about freezing their tails off in Spartan Stadium in November but it is also a whole lot more fun to freeze and be relevant.  – Steve, in Sunday’s Weather Report.

First you lose big, then you lose close, then you win close, finally you win big. – Bobby Bowden.

Join the conversation!

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Before we try to explain the above quotes, we might as well get this over with:

Because this is a Friday game, the first availability report was required on Tuesday night instead of Wednesday, in time for this preview.  So yes, we’ll be watching Cam Fancher, Kayd Coffman, and / or Leo Hannan against Oregon on Friday.

Setting the Stage: MSU vs. Oregon

Notre Dame, Nebraska, Wisconsin, UCLA. Plus many other games since 2021. The Spartans lost big. Illinois, Northwestern, and now Washington. Winnable games where Michigan State did not capitalize. Sure, it was great to see the Spartans skip ahead a step or two against Michigan but they seem to be stuck in the losing close category in the above quote.

This is an improvement over what we’ve seen the last few years but the question now is, will they revert back to step one in Friday’s game against Oregon?

Few, if any, will give MSU a chance in this one.  They will write the game off as irrelevant in what appears to be a forgettable season outside of the win at UM.  Michigan State and head coach Pat Fitzgerald can’t control what anyone outside the program thinks but Fitzgerald was adamant after the Washington loss that the Spartans would keep playing.

The team has gotten off the mat all season and, perhaps unbelievably given all the injuries, is a handful of plays from 6-4 instead of 3-7.  But, at some point, do we worry about the dam breaking?  Despite it being Senior Night for Michigan State, this seems like a real possibility against Oregon.  The Ducks, at 7-3, are fighting for their playoff life and can’t afford a loss to MSU or to Washington in their season finale.

At 5-2, Oregon is also in a three-way tie with Ohio State and Iowa in the Big Ten standings.  The Ducks are just behind second-place 6-1 Indiana.  The Hoosiers would have to lose at Washington and / or to Purdue but, if this happens and Oregon wins out, the Ducks could find their way to the Big Ten championship game playing for an automatic CFP berth.

Bottom line: Oregon still has a lot to play for. And the Spartans will need to take them on without their starting quarterback and numerous other injured players.

Here is a closer look at the Spartans’ game 11 opponent:

Oregon Season Recap

Oregon came into the season with a reported payroll in the $50 million range, ranked second, behind Ohio State, in the preseason polls, and was expected to be a serious national championship contender.  That could still happen, but Oregon didn’t do themselves any favors in the early going.

The difficulty may have began even before the first kickoff as the Ducks lost both of their coordinators from last season.  Offensive coordinator Will Stein became the head coach at Kentucky and made the Wildcats very competitive in the SEC while defensive coordinator Tosh Lupoi took over at Cal.  Both had been veterans on head coach Dan Lanning’s staff.

Lanning and the Ducks struggled to adjust and squeaked by Boise State, 34-27, in their opener. Then, Oregon had a major setback in week two, falling 39-31 at Oklahoma State. The Cowboys went 1-11 last year and fired their coach, so few were expecting a win against the Ducks this year. Now that Oklahoma State is 6-4 and one of the most improved teams in college football, Oregon’s road loss might not look so bad. But it’s still a loss.

Two weeks later, Oregon responded with a two touchdown win at USC but lost their starting quarterback, Dante Moore, on an illegal hit to the head by a Trojan defender.  Former Nebraska QB Dylan Raiola took over for Moore and threw for 289 yards against USC.

Raiola struggled the next week though as Oregon hosted UCLA. His two interceptions were part of seven total turnovers for the Ducks. Oregon turned to third-stringer Brock Thomas but it wasn’t enough, as they fell to 17-15 to the Bruins.

A 17-14 home win against Nebraska on October 17 was followed by loss number three, 21-10 at Illinois on October 24.

Since then, however, Oregon has reeled off three straight wins, including two against ranked opponents, where Raiola has played extremely well. The Ducks defeated then #20 Northwestern 34-26 on Halloween, went on the road the following week to defeat Ohio State 41-28, and are coming off a 31-7 smashing of Michigan on Saturday. Raiola has thrown for an average of 311 yards per game in those three wins.

Oregon Offense

On the season, Raiola has completed 66.2% of his passes and has thrown for 15 touchdowns.  His only two interceptions came in the loss to UCLA.

Sophomore receiver Dakorien Moore leads the Ducks with 55 receptions for 702 yards and eight TDs but Raiola has several talented options to throw to.  Three other Oregon receivers have at least 10 catches and 100 yards on the year.  Additionally, Senior tight end Jamari Johnson has 32 receptions for 405 yards and three TDs and sophomore running back Dierre Hill Jr. has 25 catches out of the backfield.

The Spartans gave up some plays through the air to Washington QB Demond Williams and also benefitted by some near misses by the Huskies.  But MSU shut down the meager Husky ground game.  Washington managed just 44 yards on the ground as MSU contained the dual-threat Williams, allowing him just 19 yards on eight carries.

This will be much harder against Oregon though as Raiola is supported by a strong run game. Hill has run for 572 yards and averages 4.9 yards per carry and is the Ducks’ primary back. Jordon Davison is right behind him with 439 yards and 4.8 YPC. Brandon Smith, Da’Juan Riggs, and Tradarian Bell are also contributing backs for Oregon.

Oregon Defense

Oregon generally ranks in the middle of the pack in most major Big Ten defensive categories. They are 10th in scoring (20.6 PPG), 11th in total defense (343.3 YPG), 12th in rushing (133.8), and 11th in passing (209.5). It’s interesting that the Ducks rank one spot behind Michigan State’s D in the last three categories but Oregon has the edge in points allowed, with MSU giving up 23.3.

Lanning, who has ties to Nick Saban and Kirby Smart and their defensive philosophies, and defensive coordinator Chris Hampton, use a 4-2-5 base defense but can switch to a 4-3 or even a 5-2 on run downs. We might expect to see a lot of this against the Spartans, especially with Milivojevic a no-go. On passing downs, Oregon can go to a 3-2-6 dime look.

Keys to the Game

So, while the defenses may be pretty equal statistically and the MSU D is improving as the year goes on, the concern has to be the Oregon offense stressing the Spartans much more than the other way around.

If MSU is going to stay in this one, they will need to produce a Michigan game-like offensive effort but finish in the end zone instead of between the uprights.  Michigan State will also need to make the plays they didn’t finish against Washington.  There was a Kayd Coffman to Frederick Moore pass along the sideline that got broken up plus another Cam Fancher to Kai Rios down the seam route that didn’t connect.  Both of these were crucial just misses in the fourth quarter.

Finally, the obvious execution mistakes – things like Fancher’s twirling around throw away attempt that was picked off, Carson Gulker’s fumble to end the game, and eight penalties for 80 yards – need to be eliminated.

Go Green on Senior Night!

msu.headline: Michigan State Film Room: The Same Old Mistakes Against Washington
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 14: The Washington Huskies offense lines up against the Michigan State Spartans defense during the second half of a college football game at Spartan Stadium on November 14, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. The Washington Huskies won the game 21-14. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

One step forward, two steps back. That seems to be the story of Michigan State football this season. Coming off an emotional victory over michigan, the Spartans opened Saturday’s game against Washington with an impressive 75-yard touchdown drive. Spartan Stadium was rocking, the offense was rolling and, for a moment, it looked like Michigan State might actually build some momentum. Unfortunately, football games last four quarters.

Before getting into the ugly, how about those uniforms? Gruff Sparty will always be No. 1 in my book, but patriotic Sparty is a close second. The American flag helmet decals and stars and stripes in the end zones looked fantastic. Even better was the crowd, which showed up in force despite watching a three-win team in mid-November. Michigan State was overmatched on paper, but with a little help from the Spartan faithful, they nearly stole another victory. The atmosphere was a fitting tribute to our veterans and another reminder that the vibes surrounding this program remain surprisingly positive. Credit Nick King of the Lansing State Journal for the picture below.

Unfortunately, good vibes don’t win football games. Coach Pat Fitzgerald acknowledged afterward that his team failed to match the physicality and intensity it displayed against michigan. Michigan State outgained Washington 342-332 and held the Huskies to just 44 rushing yards, but costly mistakes and missed opportunities proved too much to overcome in a 21-14 loss. The Spartans were good enough to compete, but couldn’t find a way to finish.

Let’s head back to the Film Room and examine four plays that explain why.

Searching for a Spark

What a difference a week makes. Against michigan, Michigan State’s offensive line looked like a group of road graders, opening massive holes and imposing its will on the wolverines. Against Washington, those same trenches became a much tougher place to operate. Pat Fitzgerald didn’t mince words afterward, criticizing his offensive line and tight ends for failing to match the physicality of the previous week. Pro Football Focus backed up his frustration, giving Michigan State its lowest rushing grade of the season (55.2).

Brandon Tullis continued grinding out 3 or 4 yards at a time, finishing with 82 yards on 21 carries, but his longest run of the afternoon was just 7 yards. Once Alessio Milivojevic went down, the Spartans desperately needed explosive plays to keep the offense moving. I’ve liked what I’ve seen from offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan, who seems to be improving as the season progresses. He’s developing a better understanding of his personnel and opposing Big Ten defenses, introducing new wrinkles and breaking tendencies to keep opponents guessing. His play calling against Washington was another step forward, including a nice end-around to Fredrick Moore. Unfortunately, those moments were too few and far between. Michigan State failed to score a single point in the second half, and without a consistent rushing attack or explosive plays to lean on, the offense struggled to finish drives.

PLAY 1: A Little Moore Creativity

With Michigan State struggling to establish its running game against Washington’s aggressive defensive front, Sheridan dialed up one of my favorite play calls of the afternoon.

Carson Gulker (No. 12) lines up in the Wildcat, a formation where we’ve typically seen him take the snap and power straight ahead through the A-gap. But this time, Sheridan breaks tendency and uses Washington’s aggressiveness against it.

Watch tight end Kai Rios (No. 88), lined up in the backfield to the right of the offensive line. Rios initially takes a couple of steps inside, selling his role as a lead blocker for another Gulker run up the middle. Instead, he quickly redirects outside to become the lead blocker for Fredrick Moore (No. 6) on the end-around.

It’s a beautifully designed bit of misdirection. Washington’s defenders attack downhill, expecting another physical run between the tackles, and Sheridan takes advantage by getting Moore to the edge for an 11-yard gain down to Washington’s 17-yard line. Against a fast, aggressive defense that’s been winning the battle in the trenches, these are exactly the kinds of tendency breakers you need. It’s a small wrinkle, but a great example of Sheridan using a defense’s aggressiveness against itself.

PLAY 2: A Red-Zone Mistake You Just Can’t Make

There’s never a good time to throw an interception, but doing it in the red zone might be the worst. After Fredrick Moore’s 11-yard end-around moved Michigan State to Washington’s 17-yard line, a costly false start by center Trent Fraley pushed the Spartans backward. Brandon Tullis gained those 5 yards back on the following play, setting up 2nd-and-10.

Michigan State lines up with three wide receivers, one tight end and one running back. Washington rushes four and appears to be playing man coverage underneath with safety help over the top. Both receivers toward the top of the formation run in-breaking routes, while Bryson Williams (No. 14) works a corner route with an inside fake. Cam Fancher (No. 2) uses play action and looks downfield, but Washington has everything covered. The safety reads the play beautifully, taking away the area where Fancher wants to find Chrishon McCray (No. 13). Sometimes you just have to tip your cap to the defense.

Watch tight end Brennan Parachek (No. 82), who chips Washington edge rusher Ramzak Fruean (No. 11) before releasing into the flat. Fruean fights through the initial contact and gets pressure on Fancher, eventually grabbing his ankle and putting the quarterback in something resembling Kurt Angle’s ankle lock. Fancher, already wearing a large knee brace after working his way back from injury, gets twisted in a direction no human leg should ever go. Rather than taking the sack, he spins around and blindly heaves the football toward the sideline, almost like a basketball player throwing an over-the-shoulder pass while falling out of bounds. Somehow, Washington linebacker Jacob Manu (No. 9) makes an incredible one-handed interception along the sideline, securing the football while staying inbounds. It’s an outstanding defensive effort from both players.

But this is a mistake Fancher simply cannot make. Sometimes the defense wins. Your offensive line gets beaten, your receivers are covered and the play is dead. That’s football. You’re not going to win every snap, but you cannot compound one bad play with an even bigger mistake. Take the sack, live to fight another down and give yourself an opportunity to put three points on the board. Instead, Michigan State walks away empty-handed from one of its best scoring opportunities of the afternoon. To make matters worse, Fancher was clearly shaken up on the play, although he eventually returned to the game.

Defensive Bright Spots and Blind Spots

One of the most encouraging developments for Michigan State this season has been the improvement of its defensive players under Pat Fitzgerald and defensive coordinator Joe Rossi. Unlike last season, when too many players seemed to plateau, we’re seeing individuals develop, gain confidence and become more comfortable within the system. Redshirt sophomore Trey Lisle (No. 8) is a perfect example, emerging as an increasingly disruptive presence along the defensive front.

Michigan State’s defense had plenty to be proud of against Washington, holding the Huskies to just 44 rushing yards on 22 attempts, an average of 2.0 yards per carry. The Spartans also recorded five tackles for loss and generated 11 quarterback pressures, although they managed just one sack. Those numbers reflect a defense that played physically and largely controlled Washington’s ground game, even if the Huskies found opportunities through the air.

But Michigan State was also missing some important defensive talent, particularly Devin Vaught (No. 2), whose instincts, anticipation and understanding of Rossi’s scheme have become increasingly valuable. Redshirt senior Aveon Grose (No. 30) stepped into a larger defensive role after primarily contributing on special teams. He held his own at times, but there were moments when his limited defensive playing time appeared to show. Against Big Ten offenses, a split-second hesitation can be the difference between a defensive stop and an explosive play.

The next two plays illustrate both sides of Michigan State’s defense. First, Lisle demonstrates tremendous effort and backside pursuit to track down a Washington ball carrier. Then we’ll examine a costly breakdown in the secondary that highlights the challenges of executing complicated coverage assignments.

PLAY 3: Trey Lisle’s Relentless Pursuit

There’s nothing overly complicated about this play. Washington runs a simple outside zone concept with running back Brian Bonner Jr. (No. 34). The design intentionally leaves the backside defensive end unblocked, counting on the running back to take the handoff, follow his blockers and hit the open running lane before backside pursuit can catch him. With a blocker out front engaging Michigan State’s defensive back, Bonner has an opportunity to turn the corner and race up the sideline for a potentially huge gain.

But Trey Lisle (No. 8) has other plans. The redshirt sophomore looks like Kenny Willekes out there, showing relentless pursuit as he chases Bonner down from the backside of the formation. Lisle covers an impressive amount of ground, refusing to give up on a play designed to run away from him, and brings Bonner down for a 1-yard loss. There’s nothing flashy about this play, just outstanding effort, athleticism and determination. It’s the kind of hustle that made Willekes a fan favorite in East Lansing and exactly what you love seeing from a developing defensive player.

PLAY 4: Too Many Moving Parts

The biggest defensive breakdown came late in the first quarter, with Washington facing 3rd-and-11 from its own 42-yard line. Quarterback Demond Williams Jr. (No. 1) connected with Chris Lawson (No. 8) for a 58-yard touchdown, tying the game at 7-7. What should have been an opportunity for Michigan State to get off the field instead became Washington’s biggest offensive play of the afternoon.

Washington does an excellent job with its pre-snap design. Watch Rashid Williams (No. 3) motion from left to right, creating a trips formation that overloads Michigan State’s coverage and forces the secondary to make quick decisions about its assignments. The motion also helps Williams Jr. identify whether the Spartans are playing man or zone coverage. Michigan State’s defenders remain relatively stationary, suggesting zone coverage.

Joe Rossi counters with an interesting defensive wrinkle. Michigan State brings a four-man rush, but defensive ends Kenny Soares Jr. (No. 1) and Anelu Lafaele (No. 11) both drop into coverage while linebackers Dion Crawford (No. 18) and Cam Stodghill (No. 12) blitz up the middle. I don’t mind mixing in something like this occasionally to confuse an offense, but it doesn’t work here. Williams Jr. has an incredible six seconds to throw the football, and frankly, he could have waited even longer. That’s an eternity on 3rd-and-11. Sometimes it’s better to let your best pass rushers rush the passer and your linebackers handle coverage.

Now watch Aveon Grose (No. 30), who seemingly runs about 75 yards on this play alone. Grose creeps toward the line of scrimmage before the snap, attempting to disguise the coverage, then retreats deep once the play begins. I suspect Grose is responsible for the coverage breakdown. He’s turned around when the quarterback releases the football and desperately tries to recover to help true freshman cornerback Jeremiah Favorite (No. 24), who appears to be expecting safety help over the top. Instead, Lawson gets behind the coverage for an easy touchdown.

I appreciate Rossi’s willingness to disguise coverages and keep opposing quarterbacks guessing, but this feels like a restaurant with a 20-page menu. There’s simply too much going on. Dropping your best pass rushers into coverage, blitzing linebackers and asking a primarily special teams contributor and a true freshman to execute complicated coverage responsibilities on 3rd-and-long seems unnecessarily risky. Sometimes simplifying the assignments puts your defenders in a better position to succeed.

And this wasn’t an isolated concern. Washington attacked Michigan State deep throughout the afternoon, and the Spartans were fortunate that Williams Jr. struggled with his accuracy. There were several occasions when receivers had opportunities downfield but couldn’t catch up to overthrown passes. With better execution from Washington’s passing game, this could have been a much uglier loss. Michigan State has made encouraging defensive progress under Rossi, but this play illustrates the importance of balancing creativity with execution.

What We Learned and What’s Next

Michigan State continues to show signs of progress, but the Washington loss exposed many of the same problems that have plagued the Spartans all season. Nick Sheridan’s play calling is becoming more creative, young defenders like Trey Lisle are developing and the defense continues to compete. Unfortunately, costly penalties, missed opportunities and coverage breakdowns remain recurring problems. The Spartans are improving, but they’re still struggling to put together four complete quarters.

Next up is Oregon, which comes to East Lansing for a Friday night showdown under the lights. The Friday night kickoff gives Fitzgerald and his staff a shortened week to prepare for another talented Big Ten opponent. The matchup also brings a familiar face back to Spartan Stadium in quarterback Dylan Raiola, better known around these parts as “Pat Mapartments.” Michigan State sacked Raiola five times and intercepted him once in last year’s matchup against Nebraska, a game the Spartans had every opportunity to win. Raiola has a different supporting cast this time around, but hopefully the Spartans can make his evening just as uncomfortable.

With the season winding down, these final games are about more than wins and losses. They’re an opportunity to evaluate the roster, develop young talent and establish the standard Fitzgerald wants to carry into next season. The results haven’t always been there, but the foundation is beginning to take shape.

If you haven’t checked it out already, here’s our latest game breakdown on The Red Cedar Rundown. We’re live Sundays on YouTube, so come hang out, give us a like and subscribe while you’re there.

You can also find me on X @W00dsyOwl. Thanks for your support!

Go Green!

msu.headline: Both Soccer Teams Selected For NCAA Tournament
msu.body:
WEST LAFAYETTE, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 13: Midfielder Kayla Briggs #9 of the Michigan State Spartans advances the ball during the 2026 Big Ten Soccer Championship game at Folk Field on November 13, 2026 in West Lafayette, Indiana. (Photo by Dave Wegiel/Big Ten/University Images via Getty Images)

The NCAA held its Selection Shows this afternoon for the men’s and women’s tournaments.  For both Spartan squads, it was not a matter of if they would make it in, but rather how good of a seed would they earn.

The Men’s Team finished their season with a 10-5-3 record after a first-round loss in the Big Ten Tournament.  Despite the early exit in that tournament, the Spartans still picked up a 4-seed for the NCAA Tournament and thus have a first-round bye in the six-round, 48-team event.

View Link

MSU will get things going this coming Sunday, November 22 at 2 PM ET, with a home game against the winner of Marshall and Bowling Green.  There is no television information at this point.  That first-round contest is this Thursday at Marshall.  If MSU advances past that, then they would go on to the third round to take on, presumably, the 1-seed in our region, Akron.

The tournament’s first four rounds are all on campus sites at the highest seeded team.  If Akron gets upset in their second-round game, we will then get to host another game.

If the Spartans can get on a run, this year’s College Cup (Final Four) is being held in Cary, NC, and will be played on December 11 and 14.

On the women’s side, our Spartans got an even better placement.  Unlike the men, the women play a full 64-team field so there are no byes.  That said, the MSU Women’s Team, fresh off a 15-4-2 campaign and a berth in the Big Ten Tournament final, earned one of the four 1-seeds and are rewarded with playing a 16-seed to get things going.

View Link

This will be the Lady Spartans 5th straight appearance in the NCAA Tournament under Coach Jeff Hosler.  We have won at least one game in each of the previous four tournaments and have made it to the round of 16 the last three seasons.  This year, we open with Central Connecticut State.  The game is this coming Saturday at 3:30 PM ET and will stream on ESPN+.

As a 1-seed, MSU would play at home as long as they advance up until the College Cup.  The women’s tournament is also ending in Cary, NC.

Since we know our football team will not be appearing in any postseason this year, let’s all give some support to what the rest of the world calls football and catch some soccer action this coming weekend as both our teams chase tournament glory.

GO GREEN!

msu.headline: Michigan State Lands Three-Star In-State Quarterback
msu.body:
Michigan State has added a quarterback in the 2028 class.

Pat Fitzgerald and his staff have been busy handing out offers in the recruiting class and have now landed an in-state product under center.

Three-star Grayson Thurston announced that he has committed to the Spartans. He made a public announcement during Saturday night’s game against Washington.

Thank you @coachfitz51 @FBCoachSheridan @CoachJ_Mc I’m proud to announce my commitment to @MSU_Football #agtg ✝️@DLSFootball_MI @coachrohn @JamesALight @AllenTrieu @C_Robinson247 @ryanobleness @JasonKillop pic.twitter.com/U1b5KE0kVj
— Grayson Thurston (@GrayThurston1) November 14, 2026

Thurston’s recruitment heated up in the summer with multiple Big Ten schools entering the mix. The product of De La Salle Collegiate High School was offered by Iowa and Minnesota over the course of two months in the summer along with Cincinnati, Toledo, UConn, Western Michigan, Bowling Green, and Miami (OH).

Thurston is currently ranked as the No. 13 overall player in Michigan. He is the 41st-ranked quarterback in the nation as well, according to 247Sports Composite.

As a sophomore, Thurston completed 62.9% of his passes for 2,009 yards with 17 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. Many who scouted him believe that he has the ability to use his legs as well — whether it be to pick up yards or navigate the pocket to get the ball downfield.

Michigan State was in on both Thurston and Brayden Tillman. As the fall went on, Thurston kept making visits on gameday including a third trip to East Lansing for Saturday’s game against Washington.

Spartan fans, how do you feel about the newest commit in 2028?

msu.headline: Cold Weather, Delayed Planes and Another MSU Loss in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 14: Alessio Milivojevic #11 of the Michigan State Spartans looks to throw the ball during the first half of a college football game against the Washington Huskies at Spartan Stadium on November 14, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The warm sunny feeling from last week has worn off quickly as MSU returns to the losing column. Frustratingly so, being that they had opportunities, faced a tired and jet lagged Husky squad and very well could have won this game. Even after last week’s victory, MSU fans found it too cold and 10 dollar tickets not enticing enough to show up for a relatively meaningless game. With that said, I better get to the report before fans stop reading.

Sun #1

Suns are always a bit tougher to find in losses. However, my first sun is going to Brandon Tullis. He racked up 21 carries for 84 yards. That is just one less carry than the entire Husky team and four yards shy of doubling their teams total rushing yards. Tullis has been phenomenal the past two weeks getting an opportunity due to injuries. His ability to keep moving forward after contact has been a difference maker in MSU’s ability to slow the game down and with the time of possession battle. Tullis is essentially the third string back and it also makes me wonder about Jace Clarizio. He was highly touted as a big get and the guy can’t seem to get a peek at the field.

Sun #2

My second sun is actually going to the offensive line. They have been the most consistent unit for the Spartans this season. Tullis is getting yards because there are actually holes. A shiftier back may be turning that into more yardage. The line is doing its job though. Giving up one sack and four tackles for losses is such a vast improvement from last year. There’s been four different quarterbacks taking snaps this season, multitudes of running backs and the line just keeps on keeping on. The one unit that had the biggest question marks coming in has shown improvement and consistency. Is it a line that will get MSU places? Not yet, not even close. It is though, trending in the right direction.

Sun #3

My third sun is a bit sad to admit, but for me it rings true. It goes to the ability to stay in games. For the most part this season MSU has managed to remain competitive for more than just a quarter or two. Washington, Northwestern, Illinois are three games that could have gone their way. They gave Notre Dame all they wanted for that game and Notre Dame is a contender for a title this year. This has not been the case in recent years. Granted some of these close losses have been at their own demise and winning those three would make them bowl eligible. If they can manage to stay healthy and pull in some better talent this team will continue to be competitive. The next step of relevance though is winning the close ones and for us as fans in those close ones to not doubt, to feel like the game is in our control. This year it feels like we’re lucky to be hanging but next year, I hope that changes.

Cloud #1

First cloud for me is going to the penalties. The terrible timing of some of these penalties is even more excruciating. The roughing the passer called on a third and forever incomplete pass that allowed Washington to continue their drive and end up going up 14-7 is a prime example. Block in the backs on decent returns, holding on solid first down runs are two others that just killed momentum and were self inflicting ways to guarantee a loss.

Cloud #2

Cloud two is most definitely headed to the turnovers. Both of those turnovers were nails in the coffin. I still have no idea what Fancher was doing on that interception. He’s had enough experience to know sometimes you have to take the sack. Twisting your knee around to throw a Kareem hook-shot into the arms of a Husky defender while you’re driving is not a smart play. Not to mention you almost tear an acl. Gulker’s fumble at the 30 second mark to end the game was almost just as bad. I know the ball was “peanut punched” but you also know that is exactly what every defender is trying to do, especially at that point in the game. I will be honest and admit I did not think they were going to march down the field and tie it up. Fitz may have even tried to go for two. Still, the way the were chipping away down the field started to give some hope until another untimely turnover squelched the game and the season.

Cloud #3

My final cloud goes to the fact that another season is over before Thanksgiving. Too many consecutive seasons without a bowl appearance is unacceptable. Half the country was still wearing masks the last time MSU made a bowl appearance. I have a child that wasn’t even born the last time they went bowling. MSU is better than that. It is a disgrace to be a university of this size and with these resources and have your seasons virtually over by Halloween. I mean, I guess nobody has to worry about freezing their tails off in Spartan Stadium in November but it is also a whole lot more fun to freeze and be relevant. The Oregon game coming up is going to be terrifying. Friday night, prior to Thanksgiving week in front of an empty Stadium on primetime and with the way the Ducks have been airing it out recently, it could be 42-0 at half. MSU needs to figure out how to stay healthy and bring in better athletes.

As always there is plenty more to complain about and perhaps even some extra suns. Maybe our best shot was for planes to have stayed grounded and the game rescheduled to a later date. I enjoy reading your reports in the comments and the discussions that they induce. With our football weather reports ending soon this season, I look forward to your comments on the Washington game. Let’s not kid ourselves though, after victories over weasels and blue devils, we knew we couldn’t keep having nice things, right?

tigers.headline: Dillon Dingler, Kevin McGonigle, and Riley Greene win Silver Slugger awards
tigers.body:
Aug 15, 2025; Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; Detroit Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler (13) and left fielder Riley Greene (31) celebrate the win over the Minnesota Twins at Target Field. Mandatory Credit: Bruce Kluckhohn-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Awards season is finally concluding for the 2026 season, and tonight the Silver Slugger awards were announced. The award recognizes the best offensive player at each position in both leagues, and the Tigers took home three of them on the night. Riley Greene won a Silver Slugger among AL outfielders, while Kevin McGonigle took home his first in the utility category. Catcher Dillon Dingler also took home his first Silver Slugger as the top hitting catcher in the American League.

The 26-year-old Greene took home his second straight Silver Slugger with a campaign that featured 21 homers in 140 games, with a slash line of .280/.370/.474 on the year. His 136 wRC+ was the highest of his career, and he was able to trim strikeouts and add walks from his 2025 production for a better all around performance at the plate. With two years remaining until free agency, questions have started to swirl around the Tigers long-term plans for Greene, but there has been no public acknowledgement of interest in an extension from either party. His status throughout 2027 will be interesting in that light, but Greene has established himself as one of the top slugging outfielders in the game even as his defensive performance has slipped each of the past two seasons.

As for Dingler, the 28-year-old catcher looked like a sure fire MVP candidate for much of his second full season in the major leagues. Already the best all-around defensive catcher in baseball, Dingler hit 27 home runs with a .243/.302/.446 slash line, good for a 107 wRC+ on the year. By the end of July, Dingler already had 23 home runs with a .269/.333/.520 slash line, good for a 136 wRC+, but between catching most games and DH-ing a lot due to the Tigers need for offense, he crashed to Earth in August and September. Hopefully the Tigers can get him off his feet a little more in 2027 and get something closer to that first half performance all season long.

As for McGonigle, not much needs be said. The AL Rookie of the Year put together one of the best campaigns from a 21-year-old in league history. He hit 18 home runs a posted a 129 wRC+ with a slash line of .278/.376/.430 on the year. He takes home the Silver Slugger in the utility category after splitting his time pretty equally between shortstop and third base, which is all the more impressive from a rookie trying to adapt to the big leagues.

No team racked up more Silver Slugger awards in either league this season. The last time the Detroit Tigers had three in a year was back in 1987, when Alan Trammell, Lou Whitaker, and Matt Nokes all won the award.

Congratulations to Riley Greene, Kevin McGonigle, and Dillon Dingler, your Tigers’ Silver Slugger award winners for 2026.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign Emilio Pagán, protect three players from the Rule 5 draft
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers outfielder Matt Vierling walks off the field after practice during spring training at TigerTown in Lakeland, Fla. on Monday, Feb. 19, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Tigers have made their moves to finalize the 40-man roster in advance of Friday’s non-tender deadline and to protect prospects from the Rule 5 draft. First, they announced the official signing of reliever Emilio Pagán on an $11.5 million deal that has an extra million in incentives based on innings pitched attached. They added three prospects, C/1B Josue Briceño, INF Peyton Graham, and INF Max Anderson to the 40-man roster. To clear four spots, OF Matt Vierling, LHP Jake Miller, 1B/2B Jace Jung, and SS Trey Sweeney were all designated for assignment.

We expected that Jung and Sweeney were on the chopping block. The former couldn’t crack the Tigers roster this season despite the huge injury issues they had in the first half of the season. Sweeney just hasn’t been able to get the bat going since the Tigers traded for him in 2024, and he missed the whole season due to shoulder surgery. Jung needs a new home where perhaps he can get some shots at the big leagues again. Sweeney is a solid candidate to sign a minor league deal if the Tigers are interested in keeping him for depth and seeing how he looks once he’s fully rehabilitated.

Vierling was the obvious choice among the outfielders on the cut line. After solid work in 2023-2024, Vierling hasn’t been able to stay on the field, and he hasn’t hit when he has been healthy. Now 30 years old, the veteran outfielder is running out of time to get his career back on track, and with plenty of depth outfield options in the organization, he was certainly expendable now.

Jake Miller is a talented lefty with excellent command and one of my favorite upper minors pitching prospects in the system. However, he’s spent the last two years battling lower back and hip problems and had double labrum surgery 13 months ago to correct the issues. He was only able to get back on the mound briefly this season and then went back on the injured list for the rest of the year. Hopefully they can sign Miller back on a minor league deal. A team might take a shot on him, but there’s a fair chance he sneaks through the Rule 5 draft with his medical status so uncertain. Either way, the Tigers probably feel like they’re in good shape for lefties and could take that chance.

Because those three are injured, they cannot be outrighted to Triple-A Toledo the way Jung could, so the Tigers will have to non-tender them on Friday, and then sign them on minor league deals if they want to keep them and if the players agree.

Adding Briceño and Anderson was obvious. Both will be looked to as part-time contributors to the offense next season as they get their first cracks at the major leagues. Less so is the addition of infielder Peyton Graham. The 25-year-old long-time shortstop has struggled to add the muscle we hoped he could on draft day. Even so, he’s turned into a solid hitter who gets on base and puts his plus speed to work. He and Seth Stephenson took advantage of the one disengagement rule in the Eastern League this season and tied for the lead in stolen bases with 66.

I was a big fan of Graham’s on draft day and have hung in their with him to a degree as his stock has fallen. While I always forecast him as a probable late bloomer with the bat, the thing that has really hurt his stock the past two years has been the lack of major improvements at the shortstop position. Graham has the speed and the arm strength to play well there, but continues to be too error prone with a bad habit of throwing the ball away when on the run or pressed for time. He has played second base and even some center field, and presumably the plan is to move him more fully into utility player territory. He’s shown some ability to play center field, and the Tigers can use that versatility in a right-handed bat.

Graham has some power too, but his long swing path has made it tougher on him to drive the ball to the pull side as he’s faced tougher pitching. Still, he hit .290 with a whopping .397 on-base percentage this year, with modest power production and nine homers overall. Graham dealt with a lot of minor, nagging injuries early in his pro career, so let’s hope he really is a late bloomer.

The Tigers roster now stands at 40 players, so any other free agent moves will require a corresponding move.

The Tigers today agreed to terms with RHP Emilio Pagán on a one-year contract for the 2027 season.

tigers.headline: RHP Bryan Abreu may be the best value in the reliever market
tigers.body:
Apr 15, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Houston Astros pitcher Bryan Abreu reacts after delivering a pitch during the seventh inning against the Colorado Rockies at Daikin Park. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

While right-hander David Bednar has the best recent resume and far more closing experience, there’s still a solid case that says RHP Bryan Abreu is the best right-handed reliever left in the free agent market. As the same time, Abreu had his worst season in 2026 at the worst time possible. The result is a volatile profile that may obscure the best value play in the whole market, or indicate an impending decline for the 29-year-old right-hander. The Tigers have not been tied to Abreu, but if they’re indeed interested in Raisel Iglesias, they’re probably checking in on prices for Abreu’s services as well and the risk-reward calculation here is certainly intriguing.

Abreu has been a mainstay of the Houston Astros bullpen since 2021, and as recently as 2025 was among the elite handful of top relievers around the game. While rarely closing games, the big right-hander has generally been deployed in the late innings against the heart of opponents’ lineups to get the toughest outs in high leverage. He has plenty of big game experience and has routinely been in the thick of them with the Astros. Unlike Bednar, Abreu did not receive a qualifying offer, and so he doesn’t have that drag on his value this offseason.

A team might get one of the steals of the offseason by going after Abreu aggressively, or the could end up overpaying for a still good reliever entering a decline phase. In my opinion the first possibility is a lot more likely, but relievers are relievers. Even putting aside the injury risk for any pitcher, relievers are a pretty volatile group.

From 2022-2025, Abreu averaged a little over 97 mph with average extension and solid life on his straight, almost cutterish, fourseam fastball, and his 87 mph slider was one of the best breaking pitches in the game. He was durable, averaging a little over 70 innings per season. In three of those four seasons, his strikeout rate was roughly 35 percent, which is just about as good as it gets. His walk rate has typically been just a little on the wrong side of league averages for relievers, and he doesn’t give up many home runs despite pitching his home games in Houston. Overall he’s been one of the more dominant relievers in the game, particularly against right-handed hitters, though never quite the best.

That dominance was completely missing in action in March and April of 2026 as Abreu got off to a downright terrible start. His fastball was down nearly two miler per hour, and his strikeout rate dropped significantly while the walks and home runs piled up in the worst year of his career. He still struck out a ton of hitters, but the bad outings were pretty bad. His ERA on May 1 was 12.54. He stabilized things in May, but then had a pretty bad June that culminated with a stint on the restricted list from June 22-26 for what manager Joe Espada described as personal reasons. It wasn’t a bereavement or family emergency eligible issue, and so Abreu went unpaid for those days, and no reason every emerged for his absence.

From July 1 onward, Abreu was right back to being his old self, compiling a 2.02 ERA with a 3.13 FIP back by a 32.6 percent strikeout rate and an 11.3 percent walk rate. Not quite prime Abreu, but right back to looking like a top 10-15 reliever in the game. His fourseam velocity, which had dipped well below 95 mph at times early in the season, was back up into the 96-97 mph range. Again, not quite prime Abreu, but close enough to erase most of the ugly memories of the first three months of the season. He also added a 93 mph cutter that was new in June and July, continuing to mix that pitch into his repertoire more and more until he was using it nearly 20 percent of the time down the stretch.

Overall the whiff rates on his three pitch mix still look really strong despite the rough first half. The fourseamer had a good whiff rate of 27.8 percent in 2026, while the slider remained elite at 39 percent (down from 46.1 percent in 2025), and the cutt racked up a whiff rate of 36.1 percent.

So this leaves evaluators in something of a dilemma. The lasting impression of his 2026 season is of a reliever who got off to a rough start, perhaps had some kind of personal problem going on, and then got it together from July 1 to the end of the year, looking again like one of the better relievers in the game and even building an effective new weapon into his toolkit in the form of that cutter.

Ben Clemens at FanGraphs had Abreu ranked as the 8th best reliever in the market entering the offseason. He suggests a two-year deal worth $18 million in free agency, and that seems very reasonable. So we’ll assume it will cost something more like two years, $25 million if the Tigers actually wanted to go after him. Or perhaps a team who offers a big one-year deal with a player option for 2028 might reel him in by guaranteeing him a nice contract that stretches beyond the developing owners vs. labor fight, but with the option to turn right around and try free agency again next year.

There’s certainly more risk than anyone expected coming into 2026, but Abreu’s strong second half has reduced it to a lingering but not quite present concern. He won’t get the monster deal it looked like he might command after his 2025 season, but he doesn’t cost a draft pick the way Bednar does after getting a qualifying offer from the Yankees, and for teams who cherish those picks, he’s the number one target left among right-handers. He’ll do well, and he’s young enough to turn around and land a bigger deal in a year or two if he can prove the first half of 2026 was a one off.

tigers.headline: The Tigers need to open three spots on their 40-man roster by Tuesday
tigers.body:
AKRON, OHIO - AUGUST 03, 2025: Josue Briceño #43 of the Erie SeaWolves hits a single during the third inning against the Akron RubberDucks at Canal Park on August 03, 2025 in Akron, Ohio. (Photo by George Kubas/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images

By Tuesday, November 17 at 6:00 p.m. ET, all MLB clubs have to finalize their 40-man rosters. Prospects that need to be protected from the Rule 5 draft have to be added, and teams have to make space to do so by designated other players for assignment. The Detroit Tigers don’t have to make many additions this year, but with the roster full, there will be a few key decisions for the front office to make.

The Tigers haven’t officially signed reliever Emilio Pagán. That deal is just pending the physical, but presumably that’s already done and they’re just waiting until the last minute to officially announce the deal and a corresponding move to open a spot on the 40-man for the veteran right-hander. So they need to open one spot already. Let’s take a look at which prospects need to be added, and who are the likely cuts to open their roster spots.

The two certainties here are catcher Josue Briceño and infielder Max Anderson. Both are far too good to be left unprotected, and both could be significant additions for the Tigers’ offense in 2027. Briceño endured a tough season of injuries, missing the first half with a right wrist injury that required surgery, and then missing all of September with an ankle injury. In between he was promoted to Triple-A Toledo but only got in 15 games before the ankle injury on August 29 ended his season. Still, Briceño is the best all-around hitter in the system and boasts all fields power. Whether the six-foot-four 22-year-old stays at catcher or moves full-time to first base remains an open question, though we suspect the latter, but either way he’s a top 100 prospect in baseball for his bat alone.

Max Anderson played a mix of second and third base this year, and while I wouldn’t put any stock in a minor league Gold Glove award, Anderson did improve in terms of just handling everything hit to him this season. His range will always make him a minor liability at second or third base, but his bat may more than make up for it. Anderson makes a lot of hard contact, and did a nice job finally becoming more selective at the plate rather than getting himself out on pitcher’s pitches. He has good zone coverage, and just needs to continue being pickier earlier in counts, looking for pitches he can drive. He may not develop the batted ball profile to get to his raw power as much as we’d like, but he’s a quality right-handed hitting infielder with minimal strikeouts whose bat should outweigh somewhat below average defensive numbers. We just need to see a little more of his hard contact in the air for power production if he’s going to develop into an everyday player.

Tigers shortstop prospect Franyerber Montilla technically needs to be added to the 40 as well but at this point he doesn’t need to be protected. Montilla is only 21 but hasn’t been out of Single-A ball yet due to a pair of catastrophic lower body injuries that cost him half of 2025 and basically all of the 2026 season. Older prospects like utilityman Peyton Graham, who lived on base in Erie and stole 66 bases this year, or hard-throwing sinkerballer Moises Rodriguez, who has stalled at Double-A trying to dial in his command, are other possibilites. With a crowded roster and more moves presumably to come this offseason, those two aren’t very likely to get added, but we’ll see. For now we’ll stick with Briceño and Anderson.

So, the Tigers need to DFA three players for starters. The most obvious options are as follows.

RHP Brenan Hanifee

LHP Jake Miller

RHP Ty Madden

LHP Enmanuel de Jesus

1B Jace Jung

SS Tsung-Che Cheng

OF Parker Meadows

SS Trey Sweeney

OF Matt Vierling

OF Wenceel Pérez

Of these options, Hanifee, Sweeney, and Jung seem like the three easiest cuts in my opinion.

Jace Jung needs to get out of the Tigers organization. There’s simply no room for him at the major league level and at best he’s still just depth at first base and can handle a little second base if needed. He’s shown zero hint that he’s going to hit at the major league level and couldn’t crack the 26-man roster this season despite the storm of injuries in April/May. It’s time to set him free to a team with at-bats available for him where maybe he can finally translate his solid Triple-A performance to the major leagues.

Trey Sweeney missed the entire season with shoulder surgery and has done nothing at the plate since the Tigers traded for him at the 2024 trade deadline. We’ll always have a few good memories of Sweeney from that insane run to the postseason, but I don’t think he’s getting claimed by anyone at this point anyway. There’s a pretty good chance he clears waivers and ends up back in Toledo anyway.

The Tigers don’t want to lose pitching depth, but Brenan Hanifee had a rough year and has never struck out enough hitters. He is a right-handed reliever who keeps the ball on the ground, so maybe the Tigers will go another direction, but they’re probably going to sign another pitcher to a major league deal before Opening Day and it’s just hard to imagine Hanifee surviving another cut beyond the current three required.

De Jesus certainly didn’t have the season we hoped for after a strong spring camp and a great showing in the WBC, but he’s a solid lefty with team control remaining. There’s no point DFA-ing him right now. If the Tigers badly need a spot for another pitcher at some point he might become more expendable. Likewise, Madden isn’t a crucial piece for the Tigers, but he’s talented and versatile enough to be useful in multiple roles and has options remaining.

There are obviously three outfield options in Vierling, Perez, and Meadows. Vierling and Meadows haven’t played much of the past two seasons and haven’t been good when they have been on the field. Meadows has a special carrying tool in his defensive ability, so I would imagine he’s safe and the Tigers will give it one more go to see if he can stay healthy. Vierling is now 30 years old and has been a non-entity since 2024. It’s time to move on, but the Tigers do seem to love him, so we’ll see. Finally, Perez certainly has his flaws, but he’s also a switch hitter with some pop and speed who generally keeps his strikeouts under control. Any one of the three is basically expendable, but the Tigers have a hard time letting go in these situations. I would guess at least two of them are still on the roster in spring camp.

Miller missed most of the year after undergoing double hip labrum surgeries after the 2025 season. He pitched for a while trying to rehab his way back to Toledo and was good as usual, but his velocity didn’t return all the way back to the steady 94 mph he had prior to 2025 and after 26.1 innings in the minors he got back to Double-A only to hit the injured list within a week. Whether there was a new injury, or whether they simply pushed his rehab too quickly and his hips did not agree is unknown, but the 25-year-old lefty is too talented to punt on right now.

Cheng is an interesting one. A light-hitting infielder with solid defense to offer at shortstop and second base, the 25-year-old from Taiwan doesn’t really do anything well enough to play him, but he does handle the shortstop position well enough to function as a depth player. The Tigers just traded cash to the Red Sox for him as they were going to put him on waivers anyway. It wouldn’t be that surprising if the Tigers tried to slip him through waivers at some point this offseason and we’ll assume his spot isn’t assured. At the same time, the Tigers acquired him because they see something to work with, presumably, so I wouldn’t think he’ll be one of the first three names off the 40-man roster.

You could perhaps add RHP Beau Brieske to this mix as well. Injuries have knocked him off the radar, but he returned late this season with a new and very hard curveball that intrigued me. Jackson Jobe started throwing roughly the same pitch, an 85-86 mph modern power curve, and it was nasty. On the other hand, 98-99 mph Brieske might be a thing of the past and he’s certainly not guaranteed a spot. If he’s past the shoulder injury, I’d rather give it another year considering the need for right handed relievers. On the other hand, he is out of options, which makes it a tougher proposition.

Again, decisions have to be made by Tuesday evening. The Tigers tend to wait until the last moment and see who other teams have DFA’d before making their final cuts. If there’s someone put on waivers that they’d like to claim, perhaps we’ll see them open more than just the three spots currently required to protect Briceño and Anderson while fitting Pagán into the roster.

Which three players would you DFA? Let us know in the comments or post to the Feed.

tigers.headline: Tigers checking in on veteran closer RHP Raisel Iglesias, per report
tigers.body:
Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Raisel Iglesias (26) watches the game from the dugout, Tuesday, March 1, 2016, at Goodyear Ballpark, in Goodyear, Arizona. 030116 Spring Training 264 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Rumors fly fast and furious this time of year, and with the owners planning to lockout the players on December 1, cutting off free agency until a new collective bargaining agreement is reached, things have gotten off to a fairly speedy start. Of course, a rumor could come from an agent trying to drum up interest in their client, or from a lower ranking executive just generally mentioning a player as being a fit. None of this means there’s a signing imminent, but BBWAA writer Francys Romero noted recently that the Tigers have shown interest in right-handed reliever Raisel Iglesias. That’s pretty vague, so I wouldn’t get too sold on the likelihood of a deal, but we’ll explore it anyway.

The  36-year-old right-hander has racked up 130 saves for the Atlanta Braves over the last four seasons. His recent peak was the 2024 campaign in which he posted a 1.95 ERA with a 2.65 FIP and was among the most valuable relievers in baseball. He hasn’t been quite that sharp the past two seasons, but he’s still a very good reliever and would immediately become the Tigers’ top dog.

Iglesias has had a much wilder ride than most major leaguers. A budding young closer on National teams for his native Cuba, Iglesias was caught fleeing through the mountains to try and defect. He was detained briefly but upon release escaped again and made his way to Haiti. A tryout in 2023 in Mexico City convinced the Cincinnati Reds to offer him a seven year deal worth $27 million. They tried to convert him into a starter in 2015, but abandoned that project the next season and he played out his contract with excellent success until he was traded to the Angels in 2020. They subsequently dealt him to Atlanta, where he played the past four seasons. Last year, the Braves signed him again to a one year, $16M deal and he made the All-Star gave for the first time in 2026.

Iglesias has since put together a decade plus of good to great relief work with rare consistency. In all that time, he’s posted an ERA over 2.75 just twice. Basically, he keeps the walks down, strikes out an above average percentage of hitters and doesn’t have a notable issue with giving up home runs.

SeasonIPERAFIPK%BB%HR/9fWAR202355.22.753.2629.46.51.131.0202469.11.952.6526.35.00.521.6202567.13.213.3127.46.01.071.0202660.02.553.1726.87.10.91.1

From 2020-2022, Iglesias hit a peak where he was sitting 96 mph and punching out over 30 percent of hitters he faced. He was never quite in the elite class, but he was certainly among the nastiest relievers in the game. Now he’s just plain nasty, but it’s still plus stuff with good command. He features one of the best changeups in baseball and it’s a time tested weapon at this point.

Iglesias sits 94-95 mph these days and mixes plenty of sinkers in with his fourseam fastball, which is his primary pitch. It’s a pretty unique set of fastballs in that neither pitch moves that much, but from a funky, low three-quarters, short arm slot, they’re really hard to differentiate for hitters. The fourseamer is almost a cut fastball, while the sinker tails away arm side. Add to that a firm changeup that looks exactly the same as the fourseam-sinker combo and then disappears, and you have a pitcher that really baffles hitters, gets whiffs, and rarely allows them to land their A swing.

The fly in the ointment is that Iglesias will be 37 next year, and if you’ve read my concerns about Emilio Pagán, well Iglesias is better but the same fears as velocity declines and mileage adds up apply. We’ll leave it at that. The Tigers have had no luck at all with older free agent pitchers.

Iglesias would fulfill the Tigers desire for a high leverage reliever who can handle either-handed hitters. He’s tougher on lefties, but handles right-handers just fine too. He does occasionally break out his slider against right-handers, and while he only used it 7.5 percent of the time last year it’s still a solid pitch in its own right. The changeup is the monster weapon in this repertoire, racking up whiff rates around 40 percent. The changeup and an approach based as much in deception as crazy movement or velocity might help Iglesias to continue to age well despite losing a full mile per hour off his fastball over the past two seasons. So far he’s continued to have good success. It’s probably wise to expect at least a little continued decline, but even so he’ll likely be the Tigers best right-handed arm if they sign him, unless peak Will Vest returns or River Ryan or another starter converts and dominates.

The other problem, is that while the Atlanta Braves went and spent bigger than expected to land RHP Evan Phillips, they may very well turn right around and offer Iglesias another deal. The Tigers are just interested. Probably a lot of teams are interested. The crop of good relievers this offseason isn’t exactly huge, and several names are off the board already. At this point I’d be pretty happy to land Iglesias but there is probably going to be a fair bit of competition for him now.

Right now, I’d probably put a low likelihood of this rumor turning into Raisel Iglesias to Detroit. If only because there are no particular ties to the Tigers for Iglesias. Ben Clemens of FanGraphs suggests he’ll get a one-year deal for $13 million, but also suggests that a lot of teams will be in on him. Those two things aren’t really compatible. If the Tigers want him, something like two years, $24 million might be what it would take. Some certainty for a player as a very uncertain offseason begins might be the ticket to luring him to pick the Tigers over the one year, $16 million that seems likely. We’ll see if they want him quite that much.

tigers.headline: Shortstop Angel de los Santos impressed in full season debut
tigers.body:
MIAMI, FL - MARCH 09: A flag bearer presents the flag of the Dominican Republic prior to the 2026 World Baseball Classic Pool D game presented by Capital One between Team Dominican Republic and Team Israel at loanDepot park on Monday, March 9, 2026 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Kelly Gavin/WBCI/MLB Photos via Getty Images) | MLB Photos via Getty Images

While we wait for more news from the Detroit Tigers this offseason, let’s continue our little series highlighting some of the most interesting breakouts in the farm system this year. We started with first baseman Beau Ankeney. Now let’s take a look at one of the most exciting teenagers in the organization. 18-year-old shortstop Angel de los Santos broke out of the Complex League to make a very impressive debut at the Single-A level.

De los Santos was signed out of the Dominican Republic back in January 2025. He received a solid signing bonus of $387,500 to join the club, and showcased his deep toolkit in a successful campaign in the Dominican Summer League. That got him on the radar last offseason as a name to watch as he arrived stateside. He made good on early reports with an advanced approach, good contact skills, and a nice mix of power, speed, and defensive ability.

De Los Santos didn’t exactly maul Complex League pitching, but in 51 games he hit six homers and struck out just 17.6 percent of the time, slashing .302/.373/.475. Expected to spend the summer in the Complex League, that work, combined with his defensive improvements, convinced the Tigers to push him to A-ball to finish the yeaer. He struck out more after the jump to Single-A Lakeland in late July, but he still hit three homers in 24 games and slashed .234/.314/.362 for the Flying Tigers. All that work got him squarely on the prospect radar, and FanGraphs currently has a 40+ grade on him.

His strikeout rate jumped to 26.7 percent with the Flying Tigers, but he walked 10.5 percent of the time and just didn’t get in enough games to start adapting to a major jump in pitching quality. What I really like is a solid 26.9 percent chase rate, a zone contact rate of 84.2 percent, and a swinging strike rate of 12.9 percent. Those are really good marks for a college hitter debuting, let alone an 18-year-old shortstop.

He did have more trouble with breaking stuff, splitters, and changeups than with fastballs, but that’s par for the course at his age. On the plus side, De Los Santos posted a monstrous .443 wOBA on fastballs over 94 mph. He hits with a pretty level, balanced right-handed swing, utilizing a short kick and he shows the ability to keep the barrel through the zone and can adjust to pitches in flight and still drive the baseball. His recognition against secondary stuff will have to improve, but he shows the raw hitting traits to project that it will.

De Los Santos topped out at 106.7 mph off the bat, so he’s already closing in on average raw power. FanGraphs projects him to eventually reach an above average 55 FV grade in that department. He’s probably added some muscle already to his listed six-foot-one, 161 pound frame, and while he should remain on the slender side and still speedy, there’s plenty of room on his frame to add good muscle in the years ahead.

Between the two levels, De Los Santos stole 30 bases, 10 of them in those 24 Single-A games. He’s not a burner, but he’s quick and gets to above average speed rapidly out of the batters box or on jumps to steal a base.

Defensively, de los Santos has a pretty good glove, quick feet, and an above average throwing arm. His athleticism stands out, and while he makes some mistakes of aggression on balls in play, he’s overall a pretty well rounded shortstop already.

What is harder to convey that the basic details is that de los Santos just feels like a gamer. He’s regularly doing things in all phases of the game to help his team win, and already shows a knack for great at-bats in key situations, catching opponents napping and taking the extra base, and chipping in the occasional run saving web gem. His ceiling is really high. If he had Bryce Rainer’s raw power potential de los Santos would be a top 100 prospect. Even so he looks likely to be a 15-20 homer type of shortstop with an equal number of stolen bases and probably average or a little better defense.

Angel de los Santos is very young, and we’ll need patience, but this is an exciting young talent who will be popping up quite high on Tigers’ prospect lists this year. Cris Rodriguez will continue to draw the most attention among recent Tigers international free agents, but De Los Santos isn’t far behind and has a little stronger floor due to his present contact ability. After so long with no signficant success in the international market for young talent, the Tigers finally seem to be stacking up a lot of interesting talent in A-ball and the rookie ball levels.
